entries.note: Means terrible lizard, coined in 1842 by [[see:Richard Owen]] from Greek [[from:deinos]], terrible, and [[from:sauros]], lizard; terrible meant awe-inspiring, and dinosaurs aren't actually lizards.
Worked at London's Natural History Museum and coined [[see:dinosaur]] in 1842.
Greek for lizard, which gives the -saurus and -saur endings of many dinosaur names, including [[gave:dinosaur]].
Lizard-hipped dinosaurs, with a forward-facing pubis; misleadingly, they are more closely related to birds than [[see:Ornithischia]] are.
Bird-hipped dinosaurs with a backward-facing pubis, the ornith- as in [[same-root:ornithology]]; they are less related to birds than [[see:Saurischia]] are.
Given as sharing the bird element found in [[same-root:Ornithischia]].
The correct term for what people usually call dinosaurs, since scientists consider birds to be dinosaurs too.
Means beast foot; the -pod ending refers to feet, as in [[same-root:tripod]]. The group includes [[see:Tyrannosaurus rex]] and [[see:Velociraptor]].
Means fast thief; [[see:Michael Crichton]] gave this name to Jurassic Park's raptors, really modelled on [[see:Deinonychus]], because it sounded scarier. Real ones were turkey-sized.
The dinosaur Jurassic Park's raptors were really based on, which [[see:Michael Crichton]] deliberately renamed [[see:Velociraptor]].
Cited as one source for Jurassic Park's hybrid [[see:Velociraptor]].
Intentionally changed [[see:Deinonychus]] to [[see:Velociraptor]] because it sounded scarier, and even apologised to a paleontologist for it.
In dinosaur names it means thief, from Latin [[from:rapere]], to seize or snatch; it shares a root with [[same-root:rapture]], [[same-root:ravish]], [[same-root:rape]] and [[same-root:rapt]].
Shares its Latin root meaning to seize with [[same-root:raptor]].
Shares its Latin root meaning to seize with [[same-root:raptor]].
Shares its Latin root meaning to seize with [[same-root:raptor]].
Meaning seized, it shares its root with [[same-root:raptor]].
Named egg thief because it was found near eggs, but it was probably protecting them, so [[see:James Gurney]] proposed renaming it [[see:Ovinutrix]].
Means egg nurse; [[see:James Gurney]] suggested it in [[see:Dinotopia]] as a fairer name for the [[see:Oviraptor]].
In [[see:Dinotopia]], suggested renaming the [[see:Oviraptor]] as [[see:Ovinutrix]].
The tyrannical king, unusual because people call it by its full genus-and-species name; it lived closer to us in time than to [[see:Stegosaurus]].
Three feet, an example of the -pod ending for feet seen in [[same-root:theropod]].
A large theropod with a sail on its back and a crocodile-like head, possibly a swimmer, shown fairly accurately in Jurassic Park III.
Means chicken-mimicking; in Jurassic Park it's the stampeding herd from which the T. rex grabs one.
Means different lizard because its hollowed vertebrae were unlike other known dinosaurs', not because it looked different; named by [[see:Othniel Charles Marsh]] in 1877.
An American paleontologist of the [[see:Bone Wars]] who named [[see:Allosaurus]], [[see:Apatosaurus]] and [[see:Brontosaurus]].
Chinese for dragon and a common suffix for dinosaurs discovered in China; the word is said to reflect the sound of a roar.
A Chinese-named dinosaur meaning crown dragon, ending in [[from:long]].
A Chinese-named dinosaur meaning sleeping dragon, ending in [[from:long]].
Means baby dragon, from [[from:long]], because it has only been found as an embryo still inside an egg.
A Chinese-named dinosaur meaning legendary dragon, ending in [[from:long]].
Named in 1824, the first dinosaur named before the word existed; described by [[see:William Buckland]] from Stonesfield fossils and mentioned in [[see:Bleak House]].
The geologist who first described [[see:Megalosaurus]].
Charles Dickens's novel mentions a [[see:Megalosaurus]] waddling up Holborn Hill like an [[see:elephantine lizard]].
Dickens's description of the [[see:Megalosaurus]] in [[see:Bleak House]], which the hosts think would suit sauropods better as a name.
Long-necked, long-tailed, small-headed lizard-hipped dinosaurs belonging to [[see:Saurischia]], such as [[see:Brontosaurus]] and [[see:Diplodocus]].
Means thunder lizard, named by Marsh in 1879; folded into [[see:Apatosaurus]] in 1903 but revived as a separate genus by some after a 2015 study.
Means deceptive lizard, since its vertebrae resembled marine reptiles'; named first, in 1877, so it took precedence over [[see:Brontosaurus]].
The late-19th-century fossil-hunting rivalry between [[see:Othniel Charles Marsh]] and [[see:Edward Drinker Cope]], whose hasty work caused many naming errors.
Marsh's rival in the [[see:Bone Wars]], who reconstructed an [[see:Elasmosaurus]] with its skull on the end of its tail.
[[see:Edward Drinker Cope]] reconstructed it with the skull at the tail end; also called the best-known [[see:plesiosaur]].
In 1903 he concluded that [[see:Brontosaurus]] and [[see:Apatosaurus]] belonged to the same genus.
Means chambered lizard, after the large holes in its skull; its skulls were wrongly put on early [[see:Brontosaurus]] mounts.
Means double beam, after paired chevron bones under the tail that Marsh thought unique; its pronunciation is disputed, with the BBC and the Natural History Museum differing.
The Natural History Museum's [[see:Diplodocus]] skeleton, sold as replicas; it was replaced in the main hall by a [[see:blue whale]] skeleton.
Brought up to show that splitting [[see:Diplodocus]] into its parts for pronunciation would also change how we say helicopter.
Means arm lizard, after its very long front legs, which gave it a sloping, giraffe-like stance.
Meso- means middle and -zoic animals; the era comprises the [[see:Triassic]], [[see:Jurassic]] and [[see:Cretaceous]] and ended 66 million years ago.
Means older animals, contrasted with the [[see:Mesozoic]].
From German [[from:Trias]], after three rock layers: [[see:Keuper]], [[see:Muschelkalk]] and [[see:Buntsandstein]]; in this period there was only [[see:Pangaea]].
One of the three German rock layers behind the name [[see:Triassic]].
Shell limestone, one of the three German rock layers behind the name [[see:Triassic]].
Colourful sandstone, one of the three German rock layers behind the name [[see:Triassic]].
Named after the limestone of the [[from:Jura Mountains]] on the French–Swiss border, which revealed much about the era.
Simply means chalky, from Latin.
The single huge landmass of the [[see:Triassic]], which split up during the [[see:Jurassic]].
Means roof lizard, after plates once thought to lie over its back like slates; its spiky tail end is the [[see:thagomizer]].
The spiked end of a [[see:Stegosaurus]] tail, invented in a [[see:The Far Side]] cartoon after the late [[see:Thag Simmons]] and adopted by paleontologists.
Gary Larson's comic in which a caveman lecturer coins [[see:thagomizer]].
A fictional dead caveman, presumably killed by a Stegosaurus, after whom the [[see:thagomizer]] is named.
The group to which [[see:Stegosaurus]] and [[see:Ankylosaurus]] belong, with uncertain pronunciation.
Means stiff or fused lizard; the root could also mean crooked, which would relate it to [[same-root?:angle]], but that isn't intended.
Would be related to [[same-root?:Ankylosaurus]] if its name meant crooked lizard.
A smaller relative of [[see:Ankylosaurus]] whose name means beautiful one, from Mongolia.
Bird-footed plant-eating dinosaurs, some upright like theropods, including [[see:Iguanodon]] and the [[see:hadrosaur]]s.
Means iguana tooth, as its teeth resembled an iguana's; -don in a name refers to teeth.
The Land Before Time character, who is a [[see:hadrosaur]], not an [[see:Iguanodon]].
The duck-billed dinosaurs, whose name describes thick, bulky lizards; they include [[see:Saurolophus]] and [[see:Parasaurolophus]].
Means crested lizard, a hadrosaur with a pointed crest at the back of its head.
Means nearly [[from:Saurolophus]]; it has a sweeping crest, possibly a resonating chamber.
Means winged toothless, from ptero- wing, an- no and -don tooth; a [[see:pterosaur]] with a 6–7 m wingspan that flew over the sea.
Jess's favourite dinosaur-like non-dinosaur, alligator-sized with a sail possibly for heat regulation, display or intimidation; unrelated to [[see:Spinosaurus]].
The horn-faced dinosaurs, from kerat-, horn, as in [[same-root:keratin]], and -ops, face; they include [[see:Triceratops]].
A group name that is a portmanteau of [[from:ceratopsians]] and [[from:ornithopod]]s.
Means three-horned face; once wrongly thought to be a juvenile [[see:Torosaurus]], and the source of the name [[gave:Sera]].
Compared with the -ops ending of [[same-root:Triceratops]], which there means face rather than eyes.
Contains the same kerat-, horn, as [[same-root:Triceratops]].
The Land Before Time triceratops, named after the -cera- in [[from:Triceratops]], not spelled Sarah; Jess only realised this as an adult.
Means old horn face, a one-horned ancestor of [[see:Triceratops]].
Means spike lizard, after its large spiky crest.
A small, cute ceratopsian.
Often mistranslated as bull lizard but probably from a Greek verb meaning to perforate, after holes in its frill; [[see:Triceratops]] was once wrongly thought to be its juvenile.
Means flying lizard; they aren't dinosaurs. First described in 1784 and initially thought to be aquatic with flippers.
Fish lizards, sea-dwelling, dolphin-like reptiles that aren't dinosaurs; [[see:Shonisaurus]] is a giant example.
A giant [[see:pterosaur]] with a 10–11 m wingspan, as tall as a giraffe, named after the Aztec god [[from:Quetzalcoatl]].
Means near lizard, as their bones are more lizard-like than dinosaurs'; underwater reptiles some link to the [[see:Loch Ness monster]].
Some people think it is actually a [[see:plesiosaur]].
An early-2000s Flash video featuring a magical [[see:Liopleurodon]], which introduced Jess to marine reptiles.
Means smooth-sided tooth; it was 6–7 m long, not the 25 m shown in [[see:Walking with Dinosaurs]], and it stars in [[see:Charlie the Unicorn]].
A BBC series that exaggerated [[see:Liopleurodon]] as 25 m long.
A Late Triassic [[see:ichthyosaur]] 15–20 m long, named after the Shoshone Mountains in Nevada; a non-Greek or Latin name.
Larger than any marine reptile, the biggest animal ever; its skeleton replaced [[see:Dippy]] at the Natural History Museum.
A Permian proto-turtle with widened ribs where a shell would develop; the name means good or true-backed lizard.
The joke punchline "do you think he saw us", for which [[see:Eunotosaurus]] sounds like an alternative.
Jokingly the best-read dinosaur, but unrelated to lizards: it means treasure trove and is related to [[same-root:treasure]].
Related to [[same-root:thesaurus]].
Means good mother; it was the first dinosaur found with seemingly incontrovertible evidence of parenting, young found near an adult.
One of the Book of St Albans collective terms, meant to be silly then but used unironically now; the hosts prefer [[see:brood]] for [[see:Maiasaura]].
The word for hatchling birds, chosen over [[see:litter]] for [[see:Maiasaura]] and her young.
